review_scope: Complete419-line MCP guide read, all checklists, protocol and logging snippets, platform changes and issue-disclosure instructions. No packages/scripts/servers/traffic capture, privilege/protection changes, secret collection or public disclosure performed. Pinned examples not current protocol claims; no policy, native, rights or independent omission certification.

A former MCP debugging route is declared as a redirect.

Missing dependencies are diagnosed through library checking or independent execution; neither was run.
Working-directory issues are diagnosed with explicit cwd configuration.
The manual debug example changes to an expected working directory.
The manual debug example runs a placeholder command with arguments.
Running process without available tools is a distinct symptom from startup failure.

The source directs manual tools/list testing.
The source directs checking server tools/list implementation.
The server must correctly respond to initialize.
The server must handle notifications/initialized.
Listed tools not selected by the model are described as a separate symptom.
The vague prompt example asks about weather without naming tool use.
The clearer prompt example explicitly requests weather-tool use; no tool was invoked.
The poor description example has an unspecified tool purpose.
The improved example describes a city-weather tool and its outputs.
Tool inputSchema must be valid JSON Schema.
Required input fields must appear in the required array.
The guide identifies tool-call timeout errors as a distinct symptom.
Increasing timeout is a suggested diagnostic adjustment, not an unlimited-time policy.
The example sets timeout300000milliseconds/five minutes; this is not an adopted global limit.
Progress logging is suggested to find performance bottlenecks.
Async work is suggested as a performance option.
Blocking I/O is directed for inspection.
Streaming is suggested for long-running tools only when supported.
Parse and invalid-request errors are listed as JSON-RPC symptoms.
Debug output on stdout rather than stderr is listed as a possible protocol error cause.
Extra newline/whitespace is listed as a possible framing issue; this is not proof all JSON whitespace is forbidden.
The incorrect example logs diagnostics to stdout.
The corrected example logs diagnostics to stderr.
The source directs UTF-8 message encoding.
The source directs avoiding byte-order marks.
Each protocol message must be a complete JSON object.
The source directs one newline-delimited message per line.
The .NET executable example uses a full Windows.exe path.
The executable example supplies empty arguments.
The executable example sets a working directory.
The executable example enables all tools.
The DLL example launches dotnet.
The DLL example passes a full DLL path.
The DLL example sets its working directory.
The DLL example enables all tools.
The Windows npx example invokes cmd.
The example uses /c npx and automatic package acquisition via -y; no package was fetched.
The example passes a filesystem-server package name.
The example provides an allowed path.
The npx example enables all tools.
The Windows example describes cmd/c wrapping for npx.
Windows raw strings or forward slashes are recommended for paths.
Avoiding spaces in paths when possible is recommended.
Required path spaces need proper quoting.
The article lists newly acquired executables as possibly blocked by antivirus.
The article lists stdin/stdout processes as possibly blocked by antivirus.
The source suggests executable antivirus exclusions; this is a protection change requiring applicable approval, not authorized ingestion.
The macOS example removes quarantine metadata from a server executable; it was not executed or accepted as a safe default.
The source notes GUI applications may lack Homebrew's path.
The macOS example uses a full Homebrew Node path.
The example passes a server-script path to Node.
The Linux example changes executable permission; no permission was changed.
The Linux example checks shared libraries with ldd.
The Debian/Ubuntu example installs a placeholder library; no package was installed.
The RHEL/CentOS example installs a placeholder library; no package was installed.
The source suggests a wrapper capturing all MCP communication, which can expose sensitive payloads; no traffic was collected.
The wrapper example creates a timestamp-derived relative log name.
The wrapper captures the server path argument.
The wrapper shifts positional arguments.
The wrapper appends a session header.
The wrapper logs the server path.
The wrapper logs arguments without shown redaction.
The wrapper tees stdin to a log.
The wrapper invokes the actual server.
The wrapper appends server stderr to the same log.
The wrapper tees stdout to the log and caller without shown redaction or bounded retention.
The configuration example launches the wrapper.
The wrapper configuration passes an actual server path and arguments.
The source recommends official MCP Inspector for interactive inspection.
The Inspector example invokes an npx package with a server path; no download or process was launched.
Inspector is described as allowing test requests.
Inspector is described as showing responses.
Inspector is described as inspecting tool schemas.
The source directs checking MCP protocol compatibility with the SDK.
The initialize-response example shows protocol2024-11-05; it is a pinned-source example, not current protocol certification.
Updating the server library is suggested for version mismatch; no library was changed.
The guide requests diagnostic information when seeking help, not permission to disclose secrets or private payloads.
